Good evening, ladies and gentlemen, and welcome to tonight's debate here in the university hall. The motion before the house is as follows: this house believes that artificial intelligence should be used in schools. Few questions in education have provoked such heated discussion in recent years, and it is easy to see why. On the one hand, supporters argue that intelligent tools could personalise learning, ease the burden on overworked teachers and give pupils in remote villages access to resources once reserved for big cities. On the other hand, critics contend that relying on such technology may undermine critical thinking, raise serious concerns about privacy and widen the gap between those who can afford it and those who cannot. As your chair, I shall not take sides. What I will insist on, however, is that every speaker be given a fair hearing and that arguments be judged on their merits rather than their volume. Each speaker will have five minutes. Without further ado, I invite the first speaker for the proposition to take the floor.

Your Honour, may it please the court. Over the past week, you have heard a great deal of evidence, and I shall not keep you long. The facts of this case are remarkably simple. My client, Ms Aigerim Nurlanova, signed a contract with Steppe Line Construction to build a family home near Almaty. The agreement was clear: the house was to be completed by the end of last summer, built to an agreed standard and delivered at an agreed price. Not only was the deadline missed by many months, but the work that was eventually carried out fell well short of what had been promised. Cracked walls, a leaking roof and windows that do not close have all been documented by independent surveyors. The defendant would have you believe that these problems were unforeseeable. Yet it was the defendant, not my client, who chose cheaper materials without consulting her. A contract is a promise, and promises, once broken, carry consequences. I respectfully ask the court to find in favour of my client. Thank you.

Hello, everyone. My name is Timur, and I suppose I ought to begin with where I'm from. I grew up in Taraz, a city that, despite being one of the oldest in Kazakhstan, rarely gets the attention it deserves. These days I live in Almaty with my wife, Aliya, and our two children, whose energy, I must admit, never ceases to amaze me. By profession I'm an architect, which goes some way towards explaining my slightly obsessive interest in old buildings. Whenever we travel, I'm the one who insists on stopping to photograph a crumbling doorway while everyone else waits patiently. Beyond work, I'm a keen mountain biker, and there's nothing quite like a weekend ride up towards the Big Almaty Lake. I've also recently taken up the dombra, though my family would probably describe my progress as modest at best. As for the future, we're hoping to restore an old house in the countryside. It's a long term dream, but one worth chasing. Thanks for listening.

Good evening, everyone! Could I have your attention for just a moment? Thank you. For those who don't know me, I'm Arman, Ali's older brother, and it's my great honour to say a few words on this very special day. When Ali first told me he had met someone in Shymkent, I'll confess I didn't take it seriously. Little did I know that within a year he would be standing here, beaming, beside the wonderful Aruzhan. Aruzhan, what you've managed to achieve is nothing short of remarkable: you've taught my brother to be on time. Our parents have been trying for thirty years. Jokes aside, seeing the two of you together, it's obvious how much you bring out the best in each other. Your kindness, your patience and your shared sense of humour will carry you through whatever life throws your way. So, please, everyone, raise your glasses. To Ali and Aruzhan, to love, laughter and a lifetime of happiness!

So, you want to hear about our trip to Mangystau? Well, I have to say, it was quite unlike anything I'd ever experienced. We set off from Aktau early on the first morning, four of us crammed into a rented jeep, with no real idea of what lay ahead. Hardly had we left the city behind when the landscape changed completely. Endless white cliffs, canyons streaked with pink and orange, and a silence so deep it was almost unsettling. On the second day, we hiked to the Bozzhyra valley, which, I'm told, was once at the bottom of an ancient ocean. Standing on the edge, watching the sun go down, I genuinely lost the ability to speak. Not everything went smoothly, of course. We got a flat tyre miles from anywhere, and it was only thanks to a passing shepherd that we made it back before dark. Looking back, though, that's the moment we laugh about most. Honestly, if you ever get the chance, go.

Right, everyone, gather round the fire and settle down for a minute. First of all, well done. Today was, without doubt, the toughest day of the week, and not a single one of you gave up. Having climbed all the way to the upper lake at Kolsay and back, you've more than earned those marshmallows. Special thanks to Daniyar's group, who, despite getting slightly lost near the waterfall, kept their spirits up brilliantly. Now, tomorrow. Breakfast is at 7:30, and we'll be heading off on a gentler walk through the forest, followed by an afternoon of orienteering. Make sure your water bottles are filled tonight, not in the morning rush. A few reminders about the rules. Nobody leaves the camp after dark without telling a leader. Food stays sealed in the kitchen tent, as we would rather not invite any curious wildlife to join us. And lights out means lights out, so no whispering until midnight, please. Okay, who knows a good campfire song?

Come along, let's take the long way round today; it's far too lovely to rush. Just look at the light coming through those birch trees. Autumn in this park never fails to take my breath away. Only a few weeks ago, everything was still green, and now the whole avenue seems to be on fire with gold and crimson. Have you noticed how many people are out this afternoon? Over by the pond, an elderly couple are feeding the ducks, while a group of students, presumably skipping lectures, are sprawled on the grass with their books. I love the fact that, whatever the season, this place somehow brings out the best in Almaty. In winter, of course, it's transformed entirely, with children sledging down that very slope and the paths crunching underfoot. Mind you, spring is arguably my favourite, when the apple blossom appears almost overnight. Shall we stop at the kiosk for a cup of tea? My treat, and then we'll head home before it gets dark.

Dear diary, it's Sunday, and it has been raining since dawn. Not the dramatic, thunderous kind of rain, but the steady, gentle sort that drums softly on the window and makes the whole world feel slower. Had it been sunny, I would no doubt have dragged myself out for a run along the Ishim embankment. As it is, I've given myself permission to do absolutely nothing useful. I've spent most of the morning curled up on the sofa under Grandma's old woollen blanket, a pot of black tea with milk within reach and a novel I've been meaning to finish for months. What strikes me most is how rarely I allow myself a day like this. There's always something to answer, something to organise, someone to call. Around noon, I made a big bowl of lagman, and the whole flat smelt wonderful. Now the streetlights are flickering on, the rain is still falling, and I feel calmer than I have in weeks. Perhaps that's the point. Goodnight.

Okay, everybody, welcome to Friday Power Hour! Find yourself a space, grab some water and let's get those bodies moving. We'll kick off with a gentle warm up. March on the spot, arms swinging, nice and easy. Now, rolling your shoulders back. Excellent. Right, here's what's coming up: three rounds of squats, lunges and push ups, followed by a core finisher that, I promise, you'll be talking about all weekend. Ready? Squats first. Feet shoulder width apart, chest up, and sit back as though there were a chair behind you. Ten more, keep going! Not only are you building strength, you're also burning off a whole week of stress. Temperatures in the canyon can climb dramatically by midday, so make sure you've each got at least two litres of water, a hat and sunscreen. Please stay on the marked path at all times; the rock formations, beautiful though they are, are extremely fragile. On no account should anyone climb them for photographs. Keep an eye on the person behind you, and we'll stop regularly for a rest. Right, if everyone's ready, let's go!

This is mission control at the Baikonur Cosmodrome, and we are now in the final minutes before launch.
